---
name: claim-checking
description: Use before claiming that something is absent, unused or the only one of its kind. Says what a search proves and how to make it prove more.
license: Apache-2.0
---

# Claim checking

A search that finds nothing proves only that this search found nothing.

## Before you say "there is none"

1. Search by the identifier, not by a phrase around it. Try the spellings the language allows:
   the plain name, the quoted name, the name inside a string, the name built by concatenation.
2. Read the whole output. Do not cut it with `head` or limit the depth of the search; what you
   did not read is not evidence either way.
3. Check what the search could not see: ignored or generated folders, files outside the
   repository, configuration, tests, and other languages in the same tree.
4. Count. If the number of matches surprises you, open one of them.

## Before you say "this is the only place"

Every caller, not the first caller: search for the name, then for each alias and re-export of it.
A rule that lives in N places has N places, and the one you did not find is usually the N+1th.

## How to report

Write the claim, the search that supports it, and the limit of that search, in that order.
"No other caller found by searching `parseConfig` in `src/` and `tests/`; generated code and
`scripts/` were not searched."

---
name: review-checklist
description: Use when reviewing a change. A short checklist of what to read, what to run and what to say, so the verdict covers what it claims to.
license: Apache-2.0
---

# Review checklist

One pass. Work through these in order and write down what you did not do.

1. **The claim.** What does the change say it does? Find the sentence in the description or the
   commit. Everything below is checked against it.
2. **The diff against the claim.** Does each hunk serve the claim? Name any hunk that does not.
3. **The callers.** For each changed function or rule, find who uses it. A change that is right
   for the caller you saw can be wrong for the one you did not.
4. **The tests.** Does a test fail if the behaviour breaks? Prefer one that asserts a value over
   one that only runs the code.
5. **The edges.** Empty input, the largest input, a second call, a failure halfway.
6. **The words.** Do the messages, comments and documentation say only what the code does?

## The verdict

State it first: approve, approve with remarks, or do not approve. Separate what blocks from what
is a remark. Close with the list of what you did not check.

@mnema/code

Your decisions, handed to your agents' sessions and held at the edits they govern: append-only and signed in the repository, and checkable by anyone. Tamper-evident, not tamper-proof: what is still in the record has not changed since it was signed, and a stranger can check that without your keys and without installing this. This is the package you install: the `mnema` command line and the MCP server of [mnema](https://github.com/mnema-work/mnema), two surfaces over one record. The agent writes through MCP while it works, and the plugin in [`plugin/`](https://github.com/mnema-work/mnema/tree/main/plugin) hands the record to a session as it opens; you read, audit and verify from the terminal. It holds no domain logic of its own: the workflow rules and the proof live in `@mnema/core` and `@mnema/chain`. ## What it gives you - **A record of decisions in the repository** that agents and people write to, each fact signed and appended, in a committed tree the team shares, a private one for this machine and a global one. - **A command line** to record, read, move work through its gates and verify, and **an MCP server** over stdio for the agent to do the same: both ask the same gate. At a terminal, `mnema decision review` goes through the decisions awaiting a judgement one by one (accept, reject, skip or quit), with no id to copy, and signs each verdict with your own key. - **`mnema init`**, which founds the record and leaves in `.mnema/` a `README.md` that says what the folder is and an `.editorconfig` that unsets what an outer one could impose on its bytes; where the repository has a `.prettierignore` or declares prettier, it adds the line `.mnema/` to it and says so; where a Biome configuration does not leave `.mnema/` alone, it ends by saying the entries to add. It writes the mnema instructions (when to call the mnema tools, and what never goes in the record) into `AGENTS.md`, into a `CLAUDE.md` or `GEMINI.md` that exists, and into a rule file of its own for Claude Code, Copilot and Cursor, and names each file. At a terminal it first shows what it found around the folder, asks which agent hosts to write them for (arrows and space; the hosts found are checked; Esc founds nothing) and whether an agent may accept what you choose, and shows everything it will write, once, before it writes any of it; with no terminal, or with `--all-hosts` or `--yes`, it asks nothing and writes all four (an agent whose shell is a pseudo-terminal passes `--all-hosts` or `--yes`, or it waits at the question). Run again in a project founded before, it adds only what that project lacks beside the record; `mnema instructions`, with `--check` or `--remove`, writes, checks or removes the instructions. `mnema doctor` points at a missing README, `.prettierignore` line or instructions block, names a pre-commit hook, Biome, dprint or lint-staged configuration that would rewrite the record, and edits none of those files. - **Tasks that carry their words.** The `--description` of `task create` and the `--brief` of `task handoff` (and the same two arguments of the `create_task` and `record_handoff` tools) record up to 64 KiB of text beside the task, as a note about it; `mnema show ` serves the description, the last handoff with its brief and the notes, and the opening read says who has each task in flight and what happened last. A handoff that names no tree is recorded where its task lives. The format does not change. - **`mnema verify`**, which reads the record with no key and no network and prints the level it reached. A record a formatter rewrote is refused, and one line beside the refusal names the files, when reading them back in canonical form proves that is all that happened. An agent key one tree of the project retired is retired in the others it reads: what the key signed there after the retirement is refused, and not counted as attested. - **A brief and a plugin** that hand the decisions in force to an agent's session, and the rules addressed at a file beside a write to it (in Claude Code, Codex, Copilot CLI, Gemini CLI, Qwen Code and OpenCode). In Claude Code the plugin also hands the brief to a subagent as it starts, and, after a question the agent asked the person is answered, names the tool that records the choice. After a write there, a note of Claude Code's own memory for this project is copied into this machine's private tree, once per content (never the index `MEMORY.md`, never a note about the person, never the public tree; on until `mnema switch off host-memory-mirror`), and a file that holds decisions the record cites nowhere gets one line naming the command that imports it, which records nothing. When the `mnema` on the `PATH` is older than the plugin, the opening of the session says so and gives the command that fixes it; `mnema doctor` says it in either direction. - **A record inherited from another repository** (`mnema inherit set`), pinned at one commit and read only when it verifies there: its rules in force reach the paths they address, in `mnema rules`, `mnema why`, `governing_rules` and the gate before a write, each naming its origin and commit. - **`mnema usage --tools`**, which counts how many times each MCP tool was called, from a file this machine keeps in its home and never in the repository; `mnema switch off tool-call-count` stops it. - **A session journal**, which the `Stop` hook keeps on this machine, outside the record: ids and counts of what a session did with it (never its words), so the next `Stop` reads only what the host wrote since and the run the MCP server closes ends with an outcome that the `resume` and `status` readings print, and the notes the next session opens with say where this one stopped; a conversation that was compacted is handed back what entered the record while its session ran. `mnema switch off session-journal`, `last-session` and `after-a-compaction` stop them. - **A task for the work a session hands to other agents**, in the Claude Code plugin: the first dispatch of a session records one private task, each dispatch a private handoff on it (its short description and the path of a brief file, never the prompt), and the end of the session closes it; `mnema switch off agent-mirror` stops it. [Every switch](https://github.com/mnema-work/mnema/blob/main/docs/switches.md) says where it begins and what it carries. [The reference](https://github.com/mnema-work/mnema/blob/main/docs/cli-reference.md) has every verb and tool, and what each one leaves unproven. ## What it proves, and what it does not The record is **tamper-evident, not tamper-proof**: it does not stop an edit, and `mnema verify` shows when what is in the record has changed since it was signed, and a cut that leaves the last checkpoint in place; by default it does not catch a cut off the end that takes the last checkpoint with it, or one tail deleted whole while another remains (a key left without a tail is noted, not failed). A record in which no tail holds anything any more exits 1, by name, at every `--require`; `--since ` exits 1 when files the revision held are gone. It reads the events and public keys of the project's trees, with no private key and no network, and prints each verdict verbatim. - It does not say every event is signed: the verdict names the level it reached, and only `verified (T1/T2/T4)` means every event is covered. - It does not catch someone holding the signing key who rewrites and signs again; a witness outside the machine (`mnema witness stamp`) dates the record, and the history a git remote keeps is what shows a cut. - It does not prove nothing was deleted: a tail removed together with its key, while another remains, leaves nothing on disk to cross. - It does not make the agent named on a fact the one that did the work, and it is not access control: anyone who can run the command line writes as this machine's identity. - It does not count every use of a tool: `mnema usage --tools` counts only the calls this machine's MCP server answered, nothing of it is signed, and `verify` does not read it. The whole table, claim by claim, is in [What it proves](https://github.com/mnema-work/mnema/blob/main/docs/what-it-proves.md), and the long form of each row is in [the reference](https://github.com/mnema-work/mnema/blob/main/docs/cli-reference.md#what-it-proves-and-what-it-does-not). ## Install ```sh npm i -g @mnema/code ``` Then `mnema doctor` says whether the `mnema` your shell runs is the one you meant. [Where the package came from](https://github.com/mnema-work/mnema/blob/main/docs/install.md#where-the-package-came-from) says how to check the published version against its npm provenance. [The install page](https://github.com/mnema-work/mnema/blob/main/docs/install.md) has the steps for a Node installed by the system. Requires Node 24.15.0 or a later 24, or 26.0.0 or later; the package is ESM-only. ## Your first record ```sh cd your-repository mnema init mnema decision record "Use SQLite for the projection cache" \ "It is embedded, it is fast enough at our sizes, and it needs no service." mnema verify ``` [Your first record](https://github.com/mnema-work/mnema/blob/main/docs/first-record.md) shows what each of them prints, line by line. ## Where to go next [The reference](https://github.com/mnema-work/mnema/blob/main/docs/cli-reference.md) · [Each host](https://github.com/mnema-work/mnema/blob/main/docs/agent-hosts.md) · [How it works](https://github.com/mnema-work/mnema/blob/main/docs/how-it-works.md) · [The plugin](https://github.com/mnema-work/mnema/blob/main/plugin/README.md) · [Where it fits](https://github.com/mnema-work/mnema/blob/main/docs/where-it-fits.md) · [Evidence](https://github.com/mnema-work/mnema/blob/main/docs/evidence.md) ## License Apache-2.0. ---
name: investigator
description: Reads code and answers a question with findings anchored to file and line. Read-only; changes nothing.
tools: Read, Grep, Glob
---

You answer one question about a codebase, and you change nothing.

- Search by the identifier the question names, read the whole output, and open the files the
  matches point to before you conclude anything.
- Report each finding as `path:line` with the line you read. A finding with no location is a
  guess; say so, or leave it out.
- Say what you searched for and what you did not search. "No match" is a result of that search,
  not a fact about the codebase.
- Follow the `claim-checking` skill for every claim of absence or of "this is the only place".
- End with the answer in one or two sentences, then the findings, then what you did not look at.

---
name: reviewer
description: Makes one pass over a change against the criteria it is given and returns a verdict. Read-only; changes nothing.
tools: Read, Grep, Glob
---

You review one change in one pass, and you change nothing.

- Ask for the criteria if none were given. Judge against what is written, not against taste.
- Read the change and the code around it. Open the files the change touches before you comment.
- Follow the `review-checklist` skill.
- Give a verdict first: approve, approve with remarks, or do not approve. Then the findings, each
  with `path:line`, what is wrong, and why it matters. Mark which findings block the verdict.
- Say what you did not check, so the verdict is read for what it covers.
